pairs.match: Structured collection of data organised into tables that model entities and relationships
wrong_matches: Software that creates and manages databases
A single horizontal entry in a table
pairs.feedback_correct: Correct! A relational database is built from related tables.
pairs.feedback_wrong: That definition belongs to a different term. Relational database refers to the overall data structure.

pairs.match: A database object storing rows about a single entity type, with columns defining attributes
wrong_matches: A named vertical field that defines a data element for every row
A minimal set of columns that uniquely identifies a row
pairs.feedback_correct: Yes! Each table represents one entity type to avoid redundancy.
pairs.feedback_wrong: That definition describes a column or a key, not a table.

pairs.match: A named vertical field in a table that defines a data element and its type for every row
wrong_matches: A database object storing rows about a single entity type
A single instance of the entity type
pairs.feedback_correct: Correct. Columns define the structure; rows hold the values.
pairs.feedback_wrong: That describes a table or a row.

pairs.match: A single horizontal entry in a table representing one instance of the entity type
wrong_matches: A named vertical field that defines a data element
The set of permissible values for a column
pairs.feedback_correct: Exactly. Each row is one occurrence of the entity.
pairs.feedback_wrong: That is a column or a domain definition.

pairs.match: Duplication of data, often from storing multiple entity types in one table, causing update anomalies
wrong_matches: The process of organizing data to reduce duplication
A description of how many instances can relate
pairs.feedback_correct: Redundancy wastes space and creates inconsistencies.

pairs.match: A category of real‑world objects (e.g., professors) that becomes a table in the database
wrong_matches: A graphical representation of the schema
An auto‑incrementing integer used as a primary key
pairs.feedback_correct: Correct. Entity types are the nouns of your data model.
pairs.feedback_wrong: That refers to ERD or surrogate key.

pairs.match: Defines the kind of values a column can hold, constraining storage and allowed operations
wrong_matches: A constraint that disallows missing values
A rule that all values must be distinct
pairs.feedback_correct: Data types are fundamental – they determine what can be stored.
pairs.feedback_wrong: Those are NOT NULL and UNIQUE constraints.

pairs.match: PostgreSQL type for character strings of any length, no maximum limit
wrong_matches: Variable‑length string type with a maximum of n characters
Fixed‑length character type that pads with spaces

pairs.match: Variable‑length character type with a maximum of n characters
wrong_matches: Fixed‑length type that always stores exactly n characters
Unlimited string type
pairs.feedback_wrong: Fixed‑length is char(n), unlimited is text.

pairs.match: Fixed‑length type: stores exactly 5 characters, padding with spaces if needed
wrong_matches: Variable‑length with up to 5 characters
A type for true/false values
pairs.feedback_correct: Exactly. char(n) pads values to the full length.
pairs.feedback_wrong: Variable‑length is varchar(5); boolean is for logical states.

pairs.match: Ensures every row has a concrete value for the column; disallows NULL
wrong_matches: Guarantees all values in the column are distinct
References a primary key in another table
pairs.feedback_correct: Correct. NOT NULL makes the column mandatory.
pairs.feedback_wrong: That is UNIQUE or a foreign key.

pairs.match: Allows multiple NULLs because NULL is not equal to any other value
wrong_matches: Automatically deletes child rows when the parent is deleted
An artificial column used as a primary key
pairs.feedback_correct: UNIQUE permits any number of NULLs in PostgreSQL.
pairs.feedback_wrong: That describes ON DELETE CASCADE or a surrogate key.

pairs.match: A set of columns that uniquely identifies rows, but may include unnecessary columns
wrong_matches: A minimal set of columns that uniquely identifies rows
The chosen unique identifier for a table
pairs.feedback_correct: Superkeys guarantee uniqueness but aren't required to be minimal.
pairs.feedback_wrong: A minimal superkey is a key; the chosen one is the primary key.

pairs.match: A set of columns uniquely identifying rows; removing any column destroys uniqueness
wrong_matches: A superkey that still works after removing columns
A foreign key reference to another table
pairs.feedback_correct: Minimality is the defining property of a key.
pairs.feedback_wrong: That would be a superkey or a foreign key, not a minimal key.

pairs.match: A key from which the primary key is selected; a table can have several
wrong_matches: An artificial column added as a primary key
A foreign key that references itself
pairs.feedback_correct: Correct. All candidate keys are keys, and one becomes the primary.
pairs.feedback_wrong: That describes a surrogate key, not a candidate key.

pairs.match: Defines the column as the unique, non‑null row identifier for the table
wrong_matches: Adds a foreign key pointing to another table
Sets the column to auto‑increment
pairs.feedback_correct: Primary key combines NOT NULL and UNIQUE.
pairs.feedback_wrong: Foreign key uses REFERENCES; auto‑increment is a separate serial type.

pairs.match: A primary or candidate key made of two or more columns
wrong_matches: A key that allows NULL values in some columns
A key automatically generated by the DBMS
pairs.feedback_wrong: Composite keys cannot contain NULLs and are not auto‑generated.

pairs.match: Column(s) that reference the primary key of another table, enforcing referential integrity
wrong_matches: A constraint that ensures no duplicate values
A column that auto‑increments
pairs.feedback_wrong: That describes UNIQUE or serial, not a foreign key.
